blocks.2: One thing that came to mean a great deal for our village, and especially for the youth society, was that the society got its own meeting hall. The opening celebration was on Sunday 26 November 1933. This was a great day that people had worked towards and looked forward to for a long time; fund-raising for a hall of their own had been going on since the youth society's first years. In 1905 a fund-raising committee was elected after a proposal in the youth society's “question box”, but as early as 21 January 1900, “Fremad”, as the society's paper was then called, no. 16, wrote about a hall of their own at Børsen.
blocks.3: The report of the opening celebration says that the party began at 4 p.m. and that about 440 people had then gathered. The menu was sour cream porridge and cured meat, and “even though there were 104 people at each sitting, there was something left at the 5th sitting”. Large quantities of sour cream collected among the farmers of the village must have gone into it. The porridge song for the party went, among other things:
blocks.5: Now we have begged and bargained for
blocks.7: every litre of cream, every cup of milk
blocks.9: and boiled from the cream a porridge so rich
blocks.10: that two or three old women floated in the fat
blocks.12: The community hall Vårtun. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.13: They had clearly got fat into the porridge even with the poor grazing the animals must have had that year, which had the driest summer in living memory.
blocks.14: It was the chairman of Noregs Ungdomslag (the national youth association), the parish priest Halvdan Freihow, who gave the opening speech. The chairman of the society, Kristian Hanssen, read a welcoming prologue. He was a driving force both in the youth society and in other things that happened in the village. It was surely he who had written both the prologue and the porridge song. Dean Hovden (then vice-chairman of the society) gave “a speech that was both thought-provoking and amusing”. Sheriff Bredvik told about the work of raising money for the hall, and the chairman spoke about “the building story”. The hall was designed by the architect Vreim, Oslo. He was attached to Noregs Ungdomslag as a building consultant. The drawings were shown at an anniversary exhibition in Trondheim that year, and the hall was considered very practical and one of the most modern meeting halls in rural Norway. It was said to be the first youth hall in the country with space for public baths in the plans. The hall had cost about 16,500 kroner in all.
blocks.15: Hovden took the floor and thanked the chairman for his efforts both in building the hall and in the society in general. Later the play “Det lagar seg nok” (It will sort itself out) was performed. The report says that “the play was well acted and was a great success”. The society's paper “Opp og Fram” was read by Leiv Midttun, and Erling Wevling read comic verses. Greetings were brought from “Vårbrud members” who had moved away, and “the easterners”, as it says in the 50th anniversary booklet, sent money and “a large primus lamp of 800 candlepower – a 30-litre coffee maker and a batch of spoons.”
blocks.16: There was a lot of singing at the party, and while the food was served in the dining room, an auction was held in the main hall. Finally the benches were pushed aside and those who wished could take a turn on the floor. Most of the benches and long tables had been made by the young people themselves. “At 2 o'clock the splendid party was over – at the end they sang ‘Aa leva det er å elska’ (To live is to love)”. The report of the party was written by Ivar L. Henriksbø.
blocks.17: Now the youth society, and the village, had a good and practical meeting hall, not only for the society's meetings and parties but also for the many other gatherings in our village. Rallies and meetings of various kinds have been held there, for the municipality and even for the county, for the Home Guard, for rifle clubs, the health association, for the bank, and not least the hall became of great use to the villagers themselves for funerals, weddings, milestone birthdays and other occasions. “Vårtun” became a beloved gathering place.
blocks.18: Most of the members in 1948, when Eivindvik youth society celebrated its 50th anniversary. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.20: One of the really big “tests” for the hall (after the opening celebration) was probably this choir festival. Part of the event was held in the community hall. The newspaper “Sogn” of 7 June 1935 has a report from the festival. The report is detailed and is a great tribute to Eivindvik and the people here, with thanks for a very well-run festival. It was the 10th festival of the Sogn choir association. There is so much praise of the village and its people here that it would be tempting to reproduce the piece in full, but that would go too far, so I must make do with a short extract.
blocks.21: It seems that Øystein Hovden's song to Eivindvik must have been new at that time. It says that the chairman of the Sogn choir association “had somehow managed to get hold of it beforehand, so it came about that the singers could greet Eivindvik with the village's own song as soon as ‘Fjalir’ came in to the quay.” “Fjalir” had been chartered as the festival boat and came to a village where “every farm and hamlet was decked out with festivities and flags” and “all homes and even more hearts stood open to receive the visitors.” “Eivindvik is an idyll of a couple of hamlets; a pearl of grace and beauty far out, where the sea has scoured so many crags hard and bare. – Yes, they knew what they were doing, the people of old who arranged to meet in Eivindvik. There they held the Gulating; from there (and a few other places) Norway emerged as a society and a state.” The reporter goes on to say that those who now held “the 10th festival itself” in Eivindvik also knew what they were doing when they brought the festival to this little village where the people are so “kind-hearted”.
blocks.22: “After singing practice in the church, and after the singers had greeted their hospitable hosts, everyone made their way to the big new community hall at Henriksbø, the finest community hall in Sogn.” About 400 people had gathered there and were received by the choir here, led by Kristian Hanssen, with “Øystein Hovden's song of welcome and tribute” – “and you can be sure they managed it! and they were greeted – warmly and sincerely.”
blocks.23: Hanssen, chairman of the youth society, bade them welcome “with a little speech that crackled with wit and fun”.
blocks.24: There were several other speeches, and since this was an anniversary celebration, the 10th choir festival, many veterans were honoured with the badge of honour made for the occasion, “a harp in the colours of the flag, stamped with S.S.; and beneath it the words: ‘Song heals’”. The first to have the badge pinned on his chest was the choir chairman, the teacher M. Volle, who also received a fine gift – a gold chain – as recognition from the Sogn choir association. It was he who had taken the initiative for the association and the festivals and “has since run everything so well in all these years”. The speech for him was given by the vice-chairman J. Aarskog, who then pinned the association's first badge of honour on Volle's chest. Chairman Volle presented the other badges.
blocks.25: The meal was in “the large and stylish dining room, where people were served the very best. All in all everything went smoothly and well, and much faster than usual on such occasions, because the whole layout and arrangement were so much more practical”.
blocks.26: The morning concert the next day was in “the large Eivindvik church”. “It became in the truest sense a service, in word and music; the church was finely decorated with flags and birch leaves.” The church was completely full and many could not get in. Dean Hovden spoke from the pulpit, the teacher Volle was parish clerk and the parish clerk Hanssen was organist. “If the singing was beautiful, the sermon by Dean Øystein Hovden was no less unforgettable. Indeed, we say plainly that it was on a level with the best we have heard from any pulpit. The sermon was masterfully conceived, shaped and delivered: it was song that rang through everything, the song from heaven, the song in human life, the hymn of praise to God's glory, the song home to God.” The programme shows that the singers performed 10 works in all, most of them well-known and much-loved songs.
blocks.27: The afternoon concert was in “the parsonage grove”. “A great crowd had then gathered, 1,200–1,500 people we guess.” “Down in the sound lay whole fleets of motorboats”. In the grove 9 works were performed in all. These were songs of a somewhat “lighter” kind. When the song programme was over, Volle gave “heartfelt thanks to the youth society and all the people of Eivindvik for an excellent reception and arrangements and everything; the teacher Hanssen thanked the singers and got the large audience to join in three times three cheers for them; Dean Hovden gave a stirring, fresh and fine speech to the singers and of farewell; M. Volle led three times three cheers for Eivindvik.” Finally everyone sang the national anthem.
blocks.28: Many of the festival crowd followed the singers to the steamer quay, where “Fjalir” waited “with flags and pennants hoisted”. “Warm and well-meant words of farewell were spoken”. “up on the height behind the church, the law-speaking rock of the old Gulating, the salute crashed out and ‘Fjalir’ answered; farewell songs on quay and boats; greetings with flags and whistles from ‘Fjalir’ and the motorboats; waving of hands and hats and handkerchiefs. They set off home from the 10th and last choir festival – the biggest and best of them all”. The church concert began at 11, the open-air concert at 3.30 p.m.
blocks.29: Øystein Hovden's beautiful song about Eivindvik is included in the report in “Sogn”, and I will reproduce it here. Hovden was priest in Gulen 1927–1937, and also dean of Ytre Sogn.
blocks.32: And the people far out here
blocks.34: who struggle for house and home
blocks.36: so hard on farm and boat,
blocks.37: sheltered from all kinds of weather.
blocks.38: you must grow fond of them:
blocks.43: With all my heart I embrace
blocks.44: That is why it is so glorious
blocks.47: True, there is sometimes dangerous weather
blocks.49: and the storm howls from the north,
blocks.50: you are so dear a place.
blocks.51: but soon in lovely clear weather
blocks.53: lie farm and hamlet and fjord.
blocks.54: you too make the heart glad.
blocks.55: Then the mind grows still as well –
blocks.59: then all the wildness is forgotten:
blocks.60: that always I must keep you
blocks.61: then Eivindvik s m i l e s.
blocks.65: so deep a note rings out
blocks.67: from the steadfast men of the past
blocks.71: H e r e history knocks at your door
blocks.73: and makes you warm and rich.
blocks.79: I believe the last verse was made especially for the song of welcome that the choir here performed at the choir festival in 1935. There has also been talk that it may have been Kristian Hanssen who wrote this verse.
blocks.82: The Gulating gathering in 1938 in the parsonage grove in Eivindvik. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.83: On 10 July 1938 a Gulating gathering was held “in memory of a thousand-year-old legal system”. The gathering was held out in the parsonage grove, in the area where the nursing and old people's home and Dr Normann's house now stand. It is called “the first Gulating gathering”. The idea of arranging such a “memorial gathering” for the old Gulating was first mentioned in “Gula Tidend” in the Christmas issue of 1937. The idea won support, and with the editor Skeidsvoll at the head of his good helpers the gathering became a reality.
blocks.84: The anniversary booklet published after the gathering, “edited by Bj. Lundeland, published by Eivindvik youth society”, says: “It turned out a lovely Sunday. All summer it had rained every weekend, but this day looked promising. There was a little shower early in the day, then the sun came out so beautifully afterwards between drifting clouds. Many people made their way to Eivindvik that day; around midday whole fleets came in through Stemnebøosen and through Folefotsundet and gathered in Prestesundet for the approach to Eivindvik. There were vessels from Flora in the north, from Vik in Sogn in the east and from Bergen and Øygarden in the south. 50–60 large motor smacks and well over fifty smaller motorboats. Fylkesbaatane sent an extra boat from Bergen to the gathering. It was ‘Nordfjord I’; she came loaded to the gunwales with people for the gathering, with music on board and a grand salute.”
blocks.85: I myself just remember this gathering and seem to recall that the whole sound was full of boats; it was like a forest of masts and “a wall of hulls”, and the road was completely full of people walking towards the gathering place. In the “summerhouse” by the parsonage, refreshments were sold, at least soft drinks, and it was said that those who stood there selling earned as much that day as they got in pay for a whole month in their ordinary work. Out at the gathering place it seemed to me like a sea of people, and I still seem to hear the shouting of the “Vikings” and the sound of their shields during the historical play. Many of the “Vikings” were “extras” from the village.
blocks.86: The ring with the court seated on the hazel-fenced field. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.87: The booklet further says that Eivindvik was decked out for a celebration, “flags at the top and people in festive mood”. The youth society's work was praised. “A row of flags had been put up along the road from the sea to the gathering place, with pennants in the old Norse colours, red and yellow. 5 huge flagpoles had been raised in a row on the isthmus facing the sound: a fluttering greeting to the sky with Norwegian flags on the sides, an old Norse flag in the middle and large pennants in red and yellow on the other two poles.” “At about 1 o'clock the gathering began, and some 4,000 people had then assembled at the gathering place. It is the largest crowd ever gathered in one place in Gulen, older villagers said.”
blocks.88: There were words of welcome from the editor Skeidsvoll, who chaired the gathering, and greetings from the mayor Henrik Tveit, who also brought greetings from the county governor Seip and from the villager now living elsewhere, “Jørgen Midttun, father of the head of national programming”. Arne Bjørndal sang the old Gulating song from Eksingedalen, Knut Robberstad gave an “exceptionally” interesting lecture on “Law and society in the saga age”. An excellent survey of legal conditions through the ages. “Mrs Vik from Vik in Sogn played some pieces on a ‘genuine Norwegian long lur’”, a “very popular item on the programme”. The piece “Mandjævningen” by Grieg was played by an orchestra from Bergen, and then came “the session”, a historical play meant to give the audience a picture of legal practice at the Gulating, and other things, about 1,000 years ago. The play was put together by the editorial secretary Skre and portrayed the inheritance case between Egil Skallagrimsson and Berg-Onund. The theatre director Lars Nygård from Bergen had staged the play and himself played Egil Skallagrimsson. After the play the head teacher Olav Hoprekstad spoke on “Saga age and present age”, “the Norwegian-American priest” O.G. Åsen from Arnafjord brought greetings from “Leif Eriksson's land”, greetings were sent from the gathering to Professor Gjelsvik in Oslo and to the people of the Faroe Islands, Sigmund Torsteinsson “read excellently ‘Sonatorrek’, Egil Skallagrimsson's beautiful lay”, and finally there were folk dance performances by the dance group of Bondeungdomslaget in Bergen.
blocks.89: In the evening there was a public party in “the big community hall in Eivindvik”. Many could not get in; “over 400 people were present at the party”. The parish clerk and teacher Kristian Hanssen gave “a lively talk on drama”, Arne Bjørndal played the fiddle and sang folk songs, Torstenson and Klaus Vabø read serious and humorous pieces, the drama group of Bondeungdomslaget performed “Hr. Sakførar” (Mr Solicitor), a “lively piece”, the dance group from Bergen gave 2 dance performances and finally Johs. Antun danced the halling. “Then Klaus Vabø gave thanks from the Norwegian-minded societies in Bergen”. In the dining room Ludvik Gjerdal thanked Eivindvik youth society, and Sheriff Jakob Eikenes thanked the people from Ervingen and Bondeungdomslaget for all they had contributed to the gathering, both with the historical play and with items on the programme at the party. At the evening party the following telegram in reply from the Faroe Islands was read out: “Norway's daughter greets you. Johannes Paturson”.
blocks.90: The memorial booklet on the 1938 Gulating gathering includes, on the first page of text, a drawing Kristian Hanssen made of the cross by the churchyard gate with the church in the background, and 3 verses of Hovden's Eivindvik song.
blocks.92: From the gathering at Flolid in 1966. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.93: The yearbook of Nord- og Midthordland Sogelag (the history society) for 1967 has a report of this gathering. That year the society had its 50th anniversary and held its “summer outing” at Flolid.
blocks.94: The gathering began around 1.30–2 p.m. with a trumpet solo (“Her er det land” – Here is the land) by Kåre Minde from Askøy. Then the mayor of Gulen, Søren Randal, opened the gathering with these words: “The assembly is in session. The lawman is in place. The Gulating gathering of 1966 is open”. He welcomed the gathering to Gulen. The chairman of the history society, Conrad Clausen, gave the society's welcome and chaired the gathering. A Gulen native living elsewhere, the teacher Benjamin Bjørklund, read the poem “Du gamle soga som stødt er ny” (You old saga, ever new) by Per Sivle. Professor Ludvig Holm-Olsen gave a historical account of the Gulating site. After the lecture the gathering sang “Dagen er komen” (The day has come) by Ivar Aasen. Professor Knut Robberstad then spoke about court sessions and legal procedure through the ages. The lawman E.T. Eftestøl took the floor and thanked Nord- og Midthordland Sogelag for showing interest in old cultural values, and for inviting him on this outing.
blocks.95: The county governor of Hordaland, Lars Leiro, brought thanks from Hordaland county, and Mayor Randal brought greetings from the county governor Schei of Sogn og Fjordane. Schei had not been able to come himself, but thanked the society for coming here and arranging this gathering.
blocks.96: Conrad Clausen thanked everyone for coming, and the gathering ended with everyone singing “Gud signe vårt dyre fedreland” (God bless our dear fatherland). According to the report, about 500 people were present.
blocks.97: After the gathering Gulen municipality invited the members of the history society who had come on the trip from Bergen to dinner “in Trygve Flolid's rooms”. Places were laid for 128 people. The menu was “cream porridge with all the trimmings, and afterwards really good coffee with kringle”. Mayor Randal welcomed them to the table, and during the meal Olav Heggelund from Dalsøyra played the fiddle. Ingrid Kidøy thanked the history society for coming.
blocks.98: “At about 9.30 p.m. we were back in Bergen. It had been a successful outing and a memorable day.”
blocks.100: Another great red-letter day in Eivindvik was Thursday 25 January 1945, when electric power was switched on in the network in our village. The issue of “Opp og Fram” for “the Festival of Light, 27 Jan. 1945” says, among other things: “And so Thursday finally dawned, otherwise like the other days; but one of the greatest days in the history of Eivindvik. We were connected to the source of light”. The editor was Ivar Henriksbø. In a piece, “Towards brighter times” by “Tobias”, there is an amusing account of all the work of getting everything ready to receive the power, and of the great disappointments they suffered time and again when the power did not come when promised. One promise after another ended in disappointment: “Yes, then there was asking and questioning and rumours flew.” “The day really did dawn when the line was finished – but the span across the fjord remained. No one had applied for permission to string it across – oh. So it was reality after all –. People stood open-mouthed – can such things be true?? Then their cheeks burned and their eyes got a dangerous gleam and less pretty words were used. The debate ran high in the shops and at the crossroads and wherever people met. So there was no light for Christmas after all, and the war did not end either.” But at the end of the piece there was great joy that we had now at last got “the light” into our houses.
blocks.101: The paper also has a fine piece about Sheriff Eikenes, who was then a prisoner in Germany, with thanks for his great work to bring electric power to Gulen.
blocks.102: I also remember well the day the power came. It was a very fine winter's day with snow and cold. I think fresh snow had fallen in the night too, and most farmers were out in the forest hauling firewood home. “Tobias” (probably the editor himself) writes that the power was switched on at 1.15 p.m. I cannot remember the time, but it was around the middle of the day. They switched the power on very gradually, from a faint glow in the bulbs to full light. I ran round all the buildings on the farm and “tried” the light, switching it on and off. It was a great delight to see the new “wonder”, light in every room. Now we no longer had to worry about not having enough oil and carbide. The carbide lamps actually gave good light as long as they had enough fuel, but at that time it was hard to get hold of carbide. For those who do not know carbide lamps, I can mention that, at least the one we had at home, looked like a cylinder, perhaps about 20 cm high. The cylinder was divided into 2 chambers: the lower held the carbide and the other ordinary water. When the water was opened so that it dripped onto the carbide, a flammable gas was produced, which was led out through a small bent pipe, about halfway up the lamp, where we then lit it. The gas gave quite good light, at least compared with what we were used to then.
blocks.103: All homes also had oil lamps, small table lamps and large, finely shaped hanging lamps, often with lots of decoration and dangling ornaments. The table lamps could also be hung on the wall and had a small brass reflector behind the lamp glass on the side facing the wall. The reflector was always polished bright and had two functions: to protect the wood behind the lamp from heat and to throw the light out into the room. The hanging lamps had a cast-iron frame and a large shade of crinkled material, often with some painted decoration. Above the lamp glass hung a small metal shield to protect against soot and sparks. The oil container with burner and glass could be raised and lowered according to where one wanted the strongest light. These large hanging lamps were a fine piece of furniture and were used in the living rooms.
blocks.104: Some had a type of lamp called a Petromax lamp. We thought these gave very good light, and they were used in workshops and other rooms where strong light was needed. As mentioned earlier, there was a large Petromax lamp in the main hall of the community hall.
blocks.105: During the war it was hard to get oil for the lamps, and the little we got was of poor quality. So it was a huge step forward when electricity came. At first it was used mostly just for light and for cooking.
blocks.106: Word spread of how splendid and successful the “Festival of Light” was. I have not found a report of the party, but in “From the history of the society” in the youth society's 50th anniversary booklet, Kristian Hanssen writes about this party: “In January 1945 a splendid ‘Festival of Light’ was held in the community hall. Almost all the adults from the whole village turned up. The board of Gulen Kraftlag, the workers at A/S Betongmast, the electricians and others were invited.” The hall shone with the many new light globes. The blackout was “sabotaged”, so the snow shone white far around. There was a prologue by Kr. Hanssen, a festive speech by Sheriff Bredvik, a choir, a lecture with slides by B. Bjørklund and speeches by the chairman of Gulen Kraftlag and by the board member Captain Norstein.
blocks.107: In the dining room there was the smell – despite rationing – of rich cream porridge, and later of “almost real” coffee!
blocks.108: Amusing and topical sketches were performed on stage, and songs were sung by Erling Wevling and Bjørklund. The party sang in unison a “light song”, which went like this:
blocks.110: The song went to the same tune as “Blant alle lande i aust og vest” (Among all lands in east and west). I remember that we schoolchildren sang it at school after the Festival of Light, and there is no doubt that the song was written by Kristian Hanssen.
blocks.111: Two other songs performed at the Festival of Light:
blocks.113: SONG FOR THE FESTIVAL OF LIGHT IN EIVINDVIK
blocks.114: These two songs were, from what I have been told, written by Erling Wevling.
blocks.115: “Tobias” (without doubt Ivar Henriksbø) wrote in the society's paper at the party that Thursday 25 January 1945 was “one of the greatest days in the history of Eivindvik”. We must surely agree with him there; look how dependent we are on electricity today – how would we have managed without it?
blocks.116: People had probably seen electric light in the village before 1945 as well. I remember well that both the sheriff and the doctor had motor-driven generators that provided light for their own household and office. In “Opp og Fram” for 29 December 1927 it seems that the sheriff got electric light at Solvang for Christmas that year. At the doctor's house it probably came a little later, perhaps around 1935, as far as people can remember.
blocks.118: Gunhild Mongstad tells: The day of 12 September 1955 had been sultry. Darkness came early in the evening. The autumn had been warm and dry with little rain. The retired couple Dina and Johannes Nygård, 77 and 76 years old, were at home on the farm at Neverdal. They were my grandparents.
blocks.119: Suddenly a flash of lightning cut through the air. At the same moment came the thunderclap that unleashed a tremendous downpour. The rain kept pouring down. Grandfather felt deeply uneasy about what might happen with so much rain after a long dry spell. There are steep mountains above the farm, and there had been landslides before.
blocks.120: Grandfather got dressed, took his torch and went out. This was around eleven at night and pitch dark. As he came out, he saw a mass of stones, branches and water come flowing and begin to build up around the house. He tried to call to the neighbour, Ida, to warn her, but had to get away himself. The slide came so slowly that he could walk away from it while shining his torch. An outbuilding and a big farmyard tree took the weight of the slide, so that it stopped against the wall of the house.
blocks.121: Inside, Grandmother heard the violent rain and became very uneasy. She went out into the hall, opened the front door and was met by a torrent of gravel, small stones and water that carried her with it into the living room. She called desperately for Grandfather, thought the slide had taken him, and was afraid she would not see him alive again.
blocks.122: Meanwhile Grandfather had made his way round the house. He saw that the slide had taken a corner of the kitchen. He cleared away some stones and got in through the hole in the wall. Grandmother was still standing in the living room in mud and gravel up to her knees. Then she heard Grandfather's voice from the kitchen. They met in the hall and got up the attic stairs, where it was dry. They held each other and wept. Mostly for joy that both were unhurt, but also in grief at what had happened.
blocks.123: Grandmother and Grandfather went to bed on the first floor. They did not get much sleep. They wondered what destruction the day would reveal after the slide. The telephone line to Guløy was broken, so early the next day the neighbour Peder Neverdal rowed over to Eivindvik and told my father Lars, my brother Johannes and Magnus Neverdal, who all worked at the slipway, what had happened. Father phoned my mother, who was at Dalsøyra cooking for a party. I did not hear about the dramatic event until late in the day. The telephone connection to Dingja was broken.
blocks.126: This happened on a Sunday. The event was marked with a gathering in the community hall in the afternoon, where this prologue was read.
blocks.128: Mayor Ola Byrknes receives the mayor's chain from Magnor Midtun. Photo: Municipal photo archive.
blocks.129: The year before the bank's centenary in 1986, I contacted the mayor about a municipal coat of arms and a mayor's chain. The agreement was that the municipality would get a coat of arms made, and the bank would then give the municipality a mayor's chain bearing the coat of arms as a centenary gift, if the bank's board agreed. The board was in favour and money was set aside for the purpose. The coat of arms was not ready until 1989, so there was no presentation at the bank's anniversary party. 17 May 1990 now stood out as a very fitting day to present the chain: the centenary of the royal decree of 17 May 1890 that changed the name of the municipality from Evenvig to Gulen. In line with quotations obtained earlier, work began on having the chain made. The chain, with the fragment of the Gulating seal (which we had had drawn for the bank's centenary) and the municipal coat of arms, arrived at the bank in good time, and on 17 May, after the service and the mayor's laying of a wreath at the memorial to those who fell in the war of 1940–45, the ceremony took place on the steps of Dahl's house, “the old town hall”, before some 300 people who had gathered at Prestebryggja.
blocks.130: The mayor, Ola Byrknes, spoke about the change of name 100 years earlier, the Byrknes and Eivindvik school bands played, and the chain was hung over the mayor's shoulders with the following words:
blocks.133: The new car ferry of Fylkesbaatane i Sogn og Fjordane, which came in 1989, was named “Gulen”. The handover and christening took place in Eivindvik on 7 October 1989. There was a grand celebration on the Sandal quay with many people present, both from the village and visitors, representatives of the shipping company, the shipyard, the county and other guests. The godmother was the mayor's wife, Mrs Ingrid Byrknes. The school band played and there were many greetings and speeches. Among those who spoke were: a representative of the shipyard that delivered the boat, the director of Fylkesbaatane, the master of the boat, the mayor of Gulen (who was also chairman of the board of Fylkesbaatane) and the deputy mayor, who presented a gift from Gulen municipality (a painting by Tom Bache-Wiig). The painting was hung in the ferry's saloon.
blocks.134: After the christening everyone could join a trip to Brekke. On board, free food and coffee were served during the trip. At Brekke the Brekke school band played. A bus had been arranged from Brekke back to Eivindvik. For invited guests the celebration continued in Førde.
blocks.135: On the quay in Eivindvik this prologue was read:
